as_told: In 1962 the Mariner 1 probe to Venus was lost because a programmer typed a period instead of a comma in a FORTRAN DO statement. FORTRAN ignores blanks and does not need declared variables, so the compiler read 'DO 3 I = 1.3' as an assignment to a new variable DO3I instead of a loop. This one-character slip destroyed the mission.
lesson: A one-character slip in code can destroy a costly mission.
what_happened: Mariner 1 was launched on 22 July 1962 and destroyed by the range safety officer 293 seconds after launch when the Atlas booster veered off course. NASA's record says two factors combined: the airborne beacon that gave rate data failed for several periods, and a superscript overbar was left out when the handwritten guidance equations were turned into computer instructions, so the guidance computer used instantaneous instead of smoothed values. The New York Times of 28 July 1962 reported the cause as the 'omission of a hyphen'. No record from the time mentions FORTRAN or a period typed for a comma. A FORTRAN DO statement with a period for a comma was found in 1963 in a NASA orbit-computation program used for the Mercury flights, according to Fred Webb, who said it caused no flight failure.
false_part: The fault was a missing overbar in a handwritten guidance equation, together with a hardware failure, not a period typed for a comma in a FORTRAN DO statement.

lesson_verdict.why: NASA's own record shows that one missing symbol in the guidance equations, combined with a beacon failure, sent incorrect steering signals and forced the destruction of the vehicle. The extra point often drawn from the story, that FORTRAN's design is to blame, is not supported by this case, because FORTRAN played no shown part in it.

confidence_note: The Myers 1976 text is quoted through Eric Roberts's transcription in RISKS 5.66; the Open Library search snippet of the book (saved) agrees with it, but the book itself could not be downloaded. The New York Times article is also quoted through that transcription. The Post Flight Review Board report was not found; NASA's NSSDCA summary is used instead. Earlier tellings than 1976 may exist. The second class, misattributed, rests on one person's recollection (Fred Webb, posted in 1989 about events of 1963); no record from the time confirms the Mercury bug.
